title: The North Face Madraque replacement poles: how to find the right pole for your 23 or 33
dek: The Madraque is discontinued, so a snapped pole can retire a good tent. Factory poles keep it pitching. Here's how the Madraque pole system works and how to match the one you need.
subject: The North Face Madraque tent poles
verdict: If your Madraque 23 or 33 has a broken or lost pole, a factory replacement is the best fix: the original DAC aluminum poles are pre-bent and cut to the tent's steep-wall geometry, which generic kits don't copy well. Match the tent model and the pole's position before you buy. A single cracked section can often be splinted in the field, but a bent or multiply-damaged pole should be replaced.
bestFor: Madraque 23 and 33 owners with a broken, bent or missing pole who want the tent to pitch exactly as designed.
notFor: Owners of other North Face tents (search your model in the pole finder instead), or anyone needing a one-off field repair rather than a new pole.
pros: Factory DAC Featherlite aluminum, the same poles the tent shipped with
Correct length and pre-bends for the Madraque's steep walls
Color-coded ends match the tent's clips and fly, so pitching stays foolproof
Keeps a discontinued, well-reviewed tent in service
cons: Each pole fits one tent model and one position, so you have to match carefully
The tent is discontinued, so supply is limited to existing stock
Without the original label, identifying a pole means measuring and counting sections

body:
## The short version

The Madraque was The North Face's roomy three-season backpacking tent, sold in a two-person (Madraque 23) and three-person (Madraque 33) version. It's been discontinued for years, but plenty are still in use, and a snapped or lost pole is the most common thing that takes one out of service.

The fix is a factory replacement pole. Madraque poles are DAC Featherlite aluminum, cut and pre-bent for the tent's unusually steep walls. A generic pole kit can get you through a weekend, but it rarely pitches the canopy as tight as the original.

## Which tents these poles fit

These poles are for The North Face Madraque only:

- **Madraque 23:** two-person, about 35 square feet of floor, 42-inch peak.
- **Madraque 33:** three-person, 90 by 66 inches (41 square feet), 45.5-inch peak.

The two tents use different floor sizes, so don't assume a 23 pole fits a 33 or the other way round. Each listing says which tent the pole is for. If you're not sure which Madraque you own, check the tag sewn inside the tent body or on the stuff sack.

## How the Madraque pole system works

The Madraque was built to feel bigger inside than its floor size. The North Face described it as abandoning a conventional pole design to get steeper walls, which is why the interior feels tall and the vestibules are large. That steep geometry depends on the poles' exact length and bends.

The poles are DAC Featherlite NSL aluminum, shock-corded so the sections snap together. Poles, clips and the fly are color-coded, so each pole goes to the matching corner and the fly lines up on the first try. The canopy hangs from the poles with twist clips rather than sleeves, which makes swapping a single pole quick: unclip it, pull it out of its corner grommets and drop the new one in.

## How to tell which pole you need

Start with what's printed on the tent. Most North Face poles and stuff sacks carry a label with the tent name, and many poles are marked with the same color as the corner webbing they go into.

If the label is gone, use these three checks against the listing:

1. **Color code.** Match the color on the pole's end tips or near the ferrules to the color on the tent's corner webbing and clips.
2. **Section count.** Count the shock-corded sections on your broken pole, including any damaged ones.
3. **Assembled length.** Lay the pole out straight and fully assembled, and measure from tip to tip. On a broken pole, measure each section and add them up.

Still unsure? Open the Help chat with a photo of the broken pole, its section count and length, and we'll match it from stock.

## Repair or replace?

Not every break needs a new pole.

- **One cracked or split section:** a pole repair sleeve (a short aluminum tube slid over the break and taped at both ends) will get you through the trip. It's a field repair, not a permanent one, because the sleeve adds a stiff spot that changes how the pole flexes.
- **Slack or snapped shock cord:** restring the pole with new shock cord. The aluminum is fine.
- **A bent section, a crushed ferrule, or more than one damaged section:** replace the whole pole. A bent section is weakened and tends to fail again in the next strong gust, often tearing the canopy clips on the way.

After any break, check the canopy clips and the fly near the damage. A pole that snaps in wind can puncture the fly.

## Is the Madraque worth keeping going?

For most owners, yes. Backpacker magazine's 2009 Gear Guide tested the Madraque 23 on a four-day trip in Wyoming's Wind River Range, where it held up in strong wind, snow and rain. Their six-foot tester and his 6-foot-7 partner both found plenty of room, and the steep walls were the reason.

Their complaints were about the tent, not the poles: the two vestibules are very different sizes, so one person gets the pack-size porch and the other gets room for boots, and condensation was higher than they expected for a double-wall tent. Good ventilation habits help: keep the vents open and crack a vestibule door on still nights.

The Madraque 33's materials are solid for a backpacking tent: a 40-denier ripstop canopy, a 40-denier siliconized nylon fly, and a 70-denier floor with a 5,000 mm coating and taped seams. A fresh pole puts a tent like that back on the trail for years.

## Bottom line

If your Madraque has a damaged pole, a factory DAC replacement is the cleanest fix, and it's the only way to get the original steep-wall pitch back. Match the tent model, the color code and the length, and you're set. For a single crack on the trail, splint it and replace it when you get home.
